title: Heavy heads give tall withers spines; heavy tails give tall lumbar-sacral spines

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Heavy heads give tall withers spines; heavy tails give tall lumbar-sacral spines

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Animals whose head and neck form a large fraction of body weight have large bending moments over the fore-legs and correspondingly tall spines over the withers, whereas animals with light heads and heavy tails (anteaters, Diplodocus) or that are bipedal (kangaroo, Iguanodon) have their tallest spines over the loins and haunches.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. XVI: On Form and Mechanical Efficiency

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: Wherever we have a heavily loaded anterior cantilever arm, that is to say whenever the head and neck represent a considerable fraction of the whole weight of the body, we tend to have large bending-moments over the fore-legs, and correspondingly high spines over the vertebrae of the withers.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter XVI, “On Form and Mechanical Efficiency”; topic “Vertebral spines and bending moments”. Scope: terrestrial quadrupedal and bipedal vertebrates, living and fossil

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch16-12: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.70

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The anatomical pattern is measurable and open 3D fossils give useful coverage. Inferred mass distributions and correlated locomotor traits make the causal bending-moment interpretation less decisive.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Across living and fossil vertebrates, estimate regional mass distribution and measure the position and height of neural spines, then test whether anterior and posterior bending moments predict spine-height maxima after phylogenetic correction.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Soft-tissue mass in fossils is reconstructed indirectly.

Muscle leverage is an alternative explanation for tall spines.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Spine profiles and rough mass distribution are recoverable from open skeletal scans for many of the living and fossil cases Thompson names. The prediction is comparative and can be fit with phylogenetic regression. Uncertainty in fossil masses and non-mechanical uses of tall spines keep the test from cleanly isolating bending moment.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Across terrestrial vertebrates, relate the craniocaudal position of the tallest neural spines to the fraction of body mass in the head and neck versus the tail. Support would be withers spines where the head is heavy and lumbar or sacral spines where the tail is heavy or the animal is bipedal; a single spinal peak unrelated to that mass distribution would refute the prediction.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Display spines and phylogeny can produce tall withers in light-headed species.

Fossil body-mass fractions are estimated from the skeleton itself, which couples the predictor to the measurement.
